title: Wait / Running Queues
explain: The two-queue model splits tasks by what they are waiting for. The Wait queue holds tasks that are not ready, waiting for a time or a resource; the Running queue holds tasks that are ready or executing. A task moves from Wait to Running when its condition is met, and back to Wait when it finishes a slice and needs to wait again. GPU serving and large-scale polling are the two classic uses.
model:
```
          condition met                    slice done, not finished
 Wait  ------------------->  Running  ------------------------------> back to Wait
 (not ready: time,           (ready or executing,                      (or done / gone)
  memory, slot)               bounded by workers)
```

User's two cases:

1. **GPU / LLM serving (continuous batching).** New requests wait in Wait (for a prefill slot and KV-cache memory). Sequences already decoding are in Running, each step emitting one token for all of them. Started work is favoured: a sequence that finishes a step goes back to the **front**, because it already holds memory and finishing frees it and bounds its latency. New requests are admitted only when capacity allows; preempted sequences go to the front of Wait.
2. **Large-scale polling.** Wait is a **min-heap on next-wakeup time**, so the top is the next job to poll. When due it moves to Running, a worker polls, and if the job is not finished it computes the next wakeup and goes back to Wait.

Cautions: no thread per sleeping job (use [trigger-based invocation](#/sd/f/trigger-based-invocation)); bound Running ([concurrency limiter](#/sd/f/concurrency-limiter)); give Running entries a [lease](#/sd/f/lease) or timeout so a crash does not make a job vanish. Plain version: [wait queue](#/sd/f/wait-queue).

details.q: A million external jobs each have their own next-poll time. What structure is the Wait queue?
details.a: A min-heap keyed by next_poll_time. The scheduler sleeps until the top is due, pops everything due and hands it to Running. A FIFO list scanned each loop is O(n) per pass, and a thread per job does not scale.

details.q: Why do LLM schedulers let running sequences continue before admitting new prefill work?
details.a: Running sequences already hold KV-cache memory; finishing them frees it and bounds their latency, while admitting too many new requests stalls everyone and risks evictions. Started work is cheaper to finish than to restart.

details.q: 1,000,000 jobs polled every 60 s, each poll holds a worker 200 ms. How many Running slots?
details.a: About 16,667 polls per second x 0.2 s = 3,333 concurrent. That is Little's law again, and it tells you the Running bound to configure.

details.q: A worker pops a job from Wait, then crashes. What is lost and how do you prevent it?
details.a: The job exists only in that worker's memory, so it is in neither queue and vanishes. Keep Running entries in the store with a lease or visibility timeout; an expired lease puts the job back in Wait.

details.q: How does the polled job get its next wakeup?
details.a: The poll result decides: fixed interval, or adaptive (poll fast while it is changing, back off while quiet; see [adaptive polling](#/sd/f/adaptive-polling) and [polling](#/sd/f/polling)). The new time is pushed back into the Wait heap.

details.q: How does this differ from a plain wait queue?
details.a: A plain wait queue just holds items until a worker is free. Here Wait is gated by a condition (time or resource), the Running set is explicit and bounded, and tasks cycle back to Wait.

prompts.q: Explain the wait / running model and give both use cases.
points: Wait holds tasks not ready, Running holds ready or executing
Move Wait to Running on condition, back when a slice finishes
GPU: prefill waits, decode runs and goes back to the front
Polling: min-heap by next wakeup, re-insert if not finished

prompts.q: Design large-scale polling of a million jobs.
points: Wait min-heap on next wakeup time
Single timer loop, no thread per job
Bounded Running pool sized by rate x duration
Lease on Running so crashes do not lose jobs

prompts.q: Explain why continuous batching favours running sequences.
points: Finishing them frees memory and bounds latency
Admit new requests only if capacity allows
Preempted sequences return to the front of Wait
